posts.author: Colin Kaminski
posts.content_md:
> **MichaelH:** Details man! Details!Your table has been left exposed to the elements?

Yeah, I have to break down all of the optics and pack them each time I shoot. I have the new table almost done and I have shot on it but I really am in the middle of a transition. Basically if you look at my website you will see the old concrete table. I have removed the cover and just have the 3.5" concrete table with the 1/2" steel plate sitting in the front of the new lab in the driveway. 

The paint on the steel is surviving very well in the rain. I would love to give this table away! The new table will be in final stages in a week or two. I am very happy with it so far. 9 layers of 1 3/8" honeycomb with a layer of 12 guage steel top and bottom, about 42 by 84". I am designing the overhead gantry now, having completed the testing of the components. I have learned much about the practicalities of using an overhead reference and the isues of moving laser beams in three dimentions. I will post photos has I have them but I am expecting to learn much about how to quickly convert between mastering and copying setups that will require adjustments to the set up.

An ideal set up for me would be not having to move the reference beam at all from single beam to H1 masters to H2 copies. This is easier on a 2D layout since moving the beam in 3d has polarization issues.

Well, I guess this ended up off topic. The work I have done outside is simply the things I would do inside. I do have access to a cool beach with sea life I could try SBR on a calm night but with a new baby I don't think that one will get done anytime soon.

posts.author: John Klayer
posts.content_md:
Other than the cave holograms, I made a few simple reflection holos with the object setting on the ground in my backyard. Details: Object on ground, Agfa 8E75 plate leaning against it, cheap red laser pointer with space filter and electric shutter mounted on a wood board on a tripod, 10 second exposure on a moonless night.

I've been working on a setup to shoot some more cave holograms using my 315. I have made some 2 beam transmission tests that capture everything in my lab on some small pieces of VRP-M and Ultimate. When I get to the cave, I want to do a larger plate such that the finished transmission hologram will be like looking thru a window into a room of the cave. I've been using a fiber to direct my reference beam and an opal glass to spread my object illumination evenly over a wide angle. I'm surprised too that the fiber works as well as it does.

posts.author: John Klayer
posts.content_md: I just made a 2 beam transmission hologram in my living room on the fireplace hearth. Why? To simulate a cave environment to try out my latest cave holography set up.

posts.author: John Klayer
posts.content_md: I took my set up for doing transmission holograms with a 315 down a north Georgia cave Sunday. Of the 14 shots I did only one has a hint of an image. My wife says she felt a slight breeze in the cave. I know 2 bats flew by and there were a few water drops falling. I'm building a portable interferometer to take back in to test the stability.

posts.author: MichaelH
posts.content_md:
> **John Klayer:** I took my set up for doing transmission holograms with a 315 down a north Georgia cave Sunday. Of the 14 shots I did only one has a hint of an image. My wife says she felt a slight breeze in the cave. I know 2 bats flew by and there were a few water drops falling. I'm building a portable interferometer to take back in to test the stability.

That's a shame you only got a hint of an image on one hologram. Was it a fairly simple setup?

posts.author: John Klayer
posts.content_md:
The set up is a 1.5 inch thick honeycomb breadboard with another .75 inch thick honeycomb breadboard for the film platten ridgidly attached to it at 90 degrees. I have an aluminum beam attached to both holding a reference mirror. The C315, a shutter, a wedge beamsplitter, a couple of mirrors and a space filter are all mounted on the thicker base breadboard. A diffuser provides the object illumination. I managed to fit this all in an empty cat litter pail with some padding to survive the rough trip into the cave. I ran the laser with two motorcycle type batteries. 

This set up worked in the lab and on my fireplace mantle. Both my digital cameras died, otherwise I'd post some pictures.

posts.author: John Klayer
posts.content_md: I'm working on making a Michaelson interferometer to take in the caves to check the stability before I waste any more film or plates. I'm asking for suggestions. What I'm building now is a laser, beamsplitter and mirror mounted on an aluminum square beam attached to a small tripod and the mirror for the other arm on another small tripod and the interference pattern projected via a lens to a screen, cave wall or a photocell and audio amplifier. Am I explaining this okay? Normally an interferometer is mounted on a holography table to check the stability by watching for no movement of the fringes. I'm wanting to seperate one mirror away from the rest of the interferometer to check the stability of the enviroment itself. Also, I'm wanting the fixed arm; the one with the laser, beamsplitter and one mirror to be somewhat short to more easily get to where I'm trying to take it. I figure that if the laser has a long enough coherence length then I can have one arm short and the other long. I started building it around a C315M then remebered that I have an Analog Tech that claims long coherence. Would a laser pointer work?

posts.author: John Klayer
posts.content_md: I finally got got my interferometer back to the same cave this past Saturday where I tried to do the holograms back in June. The interferometer indicates that the rocks are .......rock steady. I used a photo cell and amplifier to hear the fringe movements. The only sounds I could get is if I touched the interferometer components. I couldn't get a sound even if I dropped a rock right next to it. I took it back home and set it up on my holography table and got sounds by simply finger tapping the table. Maybe what Michael Harrison said about VRP-M being fogged by humidity is my problem as caves are usually about 100% humidity.

Were you developing "by eye" or by the clock? IE, were you watching the density or developing based on known required dev times computed from your exposure times?

When I first started using VRP-M I tried developing "by eye" and was under-developing the film and my images were coming out very very dim.

Is there a chance that was also happening to you?
